title: Hello, what's your name?
goal: Greet people, introduce yourself, and ask someone's name — and meet Mandarin's first surprise: a name is not linked with the word "is".
bekal: greet people and say goodbye appropriately, formally or casually
give your name with 叫 and your surname with 姓
use 不好意思 — the one phrase that gets you out of anything in Taiwan

dialogs.title: 對話 — 第一次見面
dialogs.intro: Budi, an exchange student from Indonesia, has just arrived at his university in Taipei. Outside the classroom he runs into a female student.

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.literal: you — good. I — am called — Budi.

lines.speaker: 小美:
lines.id: My surname is Lin; my name is Lin Xiaomei.
lines.literal: I — am surnamed — Lin, am called — Lin Xiaomei.

lines.speaker: 小美:
lines.text: [我也是|Wǒ yě shì]。[你是|Nǐ shì][新來的|xīn lái de][嗎|ma]？
lines.id: Me too. Are you new here?
lines.literal: I — also — am. you — are — newly — come — one — (question)?

lines.speaker: 小美:
lines.text: [哇|Wā]！[你的|Nǐ de][中文|Zhōngwén][很好|hěn hǎo][耶|ye]！
lines.id: Wow! Your Chinese is really good!

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.text: [哪裡|Nǎlǐ][哪裡|nǎlǐ]，[我|wǒ][只會|zhǐ huì][一點點|yìdiǎndiǎn]。
lines.id: Oh, not at all — I only know a tiny bit.
lines.literal: where — where, I — only — can — a-little-little.

lines.speaker: 小美:
lines.id: Sorry, what was your name again?
lines.literal: not — good — meaning, you — are called — what — name?

notes: ⚠️ **你好 is not "good morning" and not "how are you".** Literally it is "you good", and it works exactly like "hello" — any time, day or night. The reply is the same word back: *你好*.

**哪裡哪裡 is the Taiwanese way to deflect a compliment.** Literally "where, where" — meaning "oh no, I'm not that good". Accepting praise with a plain *謝謝* can sound a little smug; brushing it off first is the polite habit.
**耶 (*ye*) at the end of a sentence is very Taiwanese.** It adds a sense of pleasant surprise or admiration — roughly "wow" or "really!" in English. You'll hear it dozens of times a day in Taipei.
**掰掰 (*bāibāi*) is "bye-bye" written in characters.** In Taiwan it is far more common than 再見 (*zàijiàn*) in everyday conversation; 再見 feels slightly more formal.
⚠️ **同學 (*tóngxué*) means "classmate", but it is also a form of address** between students, combined with the surname: 林同學. Just like 老師 for teachers and 先生/小姐 for people in general.

grammars.title: 叫 and 姓: names don't take 是
body: English says "my name is Budi" — a noun ("name") linked by "is". Mandarin uses a **verb** instead, and it has two different verbs depending on whether you are giving your given name or your surname.
after: ⚠️ **我是布迪 is also correct**, but it means something slightly different: "I *am* Budi" — used when introducing yourself on stage or confirming who you are. For an ordinary introduction, 我叫 sounds more natural.
⚠️ **Never say 我是姓林.** 姓 is already a verb; putting 是 in front is like saying "I am am-surnamed Lin".
**貴姓 is the polite form**, used with older people, customers, or on the office phone. The answer is not 我貴姓林 but **敝姓林** (*bì xìng Lín*, "my humble surname is Lin") or simply **我姓林**.

grammars.title: Chinese names: surname first, then given name
body: **林小美**: 林 is the surname, 小美 the given name. The order is the reverse of Western habit and is never flipped, not even when written in Latin letters.
after: The five most common surnames in Taiwan: **陳** (Chén), **林** (Lín), **黃** (Huáng), **張** (Zhāng), **李** (Lǐ). One in ten Taiwanese is surnamed 陳.

⚠️ **Calling someone by their bare surname sounds rude.** The surname always comes with something: 林小姐 (Miss Lin), 林老師 (Teacher Lin), 林同學 (classmate Lin), or 小林 (little Lin, friendly). The given name alone is used only by family and close friends.
**阿 (*ā*) before the last syllable of a name is a typically Taiwanese term of endearment** — inherited from Hokkien. 阿文, 阿明, 阿美. It sounds warm and down-to-earth in the best sense.

blocks.text: ⚠️ The last two lines **are not interchangeable**. *慢走* (literally "walk slowly") is said by a host or shopkeeper to a departing guest; the one leaving answers *謝謝* or *再見*. It works like "take care" from the host and "bye, thanks" from the guest.

sections.title: 不好意思: the most useful phrase in Taiwan

blocks.text: If you could take only one phrase from this unit, take **不好意思** (*bù hǎoyìsi*). Literally "not-good meaning" — and Taiwanese people use it for almost every social situation.

blocks.title: Five jobs of 不好意思
items: **Excuse me, coming through** — squeezing out of a crowded train.
**Excuse me, may I ask** — before asking a stranger for directions.
**Calling the waiter** — in a restaurant, don't wave; just say *不好意思*.
**A light apology** — bumping into someone, arriving five minutes late, causing a bother.
**Saying no politely** — *不好意思，我今天不行。* "Sorry, I can't make it today."

blocks.text: ⚠️ For a **real** wrong — breaking something, hurting someone's feelings, breaking a promise — 不好意思 is too light. Use **對不起** (*duìbùqǐ*, "can't face you"). Telling the two apart is one of the quickest signs that someone actually lives in Taiwan rather than just learning from a book.

blocks.text: Learn the last sentence today. It turns everyone you meet into a teacher and everything around you into a flashcard. Point at the thing, say the sentence, listen to the answer, repeat it out loud. That is one full learning loop in ten seconds.
